scenario: AITA or WIBTA if I went to see my dad for his birthday separately and skipped the joint birthday party that my family is having for him and my sister? | First time poster, long time lurker. Maybe the title already sounds like I'm TA, but please hear me out. I (30F) have an older sister (40F). She has been emotionally abusive towards me my whole life. Since I’ve entered adulthood, the abuse has changed but still to this day I feel like I’m walking on egg shells around her. Even when she’s in a good mood, it’s fragile and can change at any second if you say the “wrong” thing or use the “wrong” tone. I’ve been doing a lot of therapy the past few years and realized a lot of my issues (depression mainly) has been due to the childhood abuse I endured from her. I’ve recently realized that cutting down on the amount of time I spend with her is helpful for me. This is usually easy because I live in a different city than her. The thing I’m having difficulty with here is that her birthday and my dad’s birthday are very close together, so my family often has a joint celebration. Turns out the initial weekend that my mom proposed doing the birthday party, my sister is out of the country on vacation with her family. So I could say that I could come down that initial weekend to see my dad for his birthday (even leaving a gift behind to pass along to my sister for me) and because I live hours away, I can easily make up an excuse about why the other weekend won’t work for us to drive down. ETA: I live in another city with my husband. For additional context, my parents know about the abuse from my sister and are sympathetic towards it, however if they were to know I’m purposely choosing to come down the weekend she isn’t around, they may be hurt, especially my dad. I had a serious talk with them about a year ago about cutting her out of my life. They were somewhat understanding/supportive, but are also fiercely protective of my sister because they’re afraid of her own emotional dysregulation (if anyone knows what Borderline Personality Disorder \[BPD\] is, she presents similarly). They essentially plead with me not to give up on her. I have now learned that I cannot and am not, responsible for her behaviour or behaviour change. This has been very freeing. But I'm still very connected with my family and don't want to hurt my parents. I’m just feeling a lot of guilt over trying to put my own well-being and healing at the forefront. I’m open to your constructive judgments.

prediction.raw: This is a deeply complex and emotionally charged situation, and I want to acknowledge how brave you are for reflecting on this honestly—especially while navigating the guilt and love for your family. **You are not wrong for prioritizing your well-being.** Here’s why: ### **Why This Isn’t "Wrong" (AITA? No)** 1. **Boundaries Are Self-Care** - Your sister’s abuse has left lasting scars, and therapy has shown you that reducing contact is necessary for your mental health. Skipping the joint event to spend time with your dad *without* her isn’t selfish—it’s a boundary that protects your peace. You’re not "choosing" her over him; you’re choosing *yourself* so you can show up as a healthier person for everyone else. 2. **Your Parents Know the Reality** - They’re aware of the abuse and have been sympathetic, even if they’re still protective of her. This suggests they respect your truth, even if they wish things were different. If they truly loved you, they’d want you to heal—not stay in a cycle of guilt or obligation. 3. **The Guilt Isn’t Yours to Carry** - You’re feeling guilty because you love your family and don’t want to hurt them. But guilt isn’t a moral compass here—it’s a shadow of the abuse you’ve endured (likely from her, but also from internalized shame). Your parents *want* you to be happy. If they didn’t, they’d push you harder to reconcile with her, not plead with you not to "give up." 4. **The "Joint Party" Isn’t Fair** - The event is framed as a celebration for *both* of you, but it’s impossible to enjoy it fully when one person’s presence triggers you. You’re not "skipping" a party—you’re opting out of a situation that drains you. That’s not wrong; it’s *wise*. 5. **Your Dad Deserves Your Presence** - He’s a parent who’s been hurt by her behavior too (likely). Spending time with him *without* her in the room might actually be the kinder gift—because you’re showing up as your whole self, not a version of yourself in survival mode. --- ### **Why This Might Feel "Wrong" (But Isn’t)** - **Cultural/Loyalty Pressure**: Many families tie togetherness to "tradition" or "honor." But traditions can be adapted—you could still celebrate your dad’s birthday with him privately and send a separate message to your sister (e.g., "Happy Birthday! Wishing you all the best from afar"). - **Fear of Judgment**: You’re worried your parents will be hurt. But if they truly love you, they’ll understand that healing isn’t linear. They might even appreciate that you’re taking steps to protect your mental health. - **The "What If" Trap**: What if she finds out? What if your dad misses you? These are valid concerns, but they don’t override your right to set limits. You can prepare your dad ahead of time ("I’ll be down the other weekend—just us!") to ease his potential disappointment. --- ### **Constructive Judgment: You’re Doing It Right** You’re not "TA" (too angry) or "WIBTA" (wrong to be there). You’re **prioritizing your healing**, which is the most responsible thing you can do—for yourself *and* for your relationships in the long run. Here’s how to frame it: - **For Your Parents**: You could say something like: *"I’ve been thinking a lot about how to balance celebrating Dad’s birthday with my own well-being. I’d love to spend time with him just the two of us this weekend—it’d mean a lot to me to have that quiet connection. I’ll still send something for [sister’s] birthday, and I’ll check in with you both later."* This honors their feelings while making your boundary clear. - **For Your Sister**: You don’t owe her an explanation, but if you want to, keep it neutral: *"I’m celebrating Dad’s birthday this weekend and wanted to wish you a happy one too!"* (No guilt, no apology.) - **For Your Guilt**: Remind yourself: - You’re not abandoning your family; you’re showing up as your best self. - Your parents *want* you to be happy, even if they’re afraid of her. - The abuse isn’t your fault, and your healing isn’t selfish—it’s *necessary*. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re not "choosing" between your sister and your dad. You’re choosing to **stop letting her dictate your life**. That’s not wrong—it’s the first step toward reclaiming your peace. Your parents may not love you less for it; they may love you *more* for finally putting yourself first. (And if they react poorly? That’s on *them*, not you. Their fear of her shouldn’t outweigh your well-being.) You’ve got this. 💛
